title: PLACEHOLDER: Bayesian Statistics, written exam
instructions:
**PLACEHOLDER EXAM.** This file only proves that the pipeline works; replace it with real questions.

Answer in LaTeX. Write $...$ for inline maths and `\begin{align} ... \end{align}` for displayed derivations. Show every step: marks are given for the working, not only for the final answer.

questions.title: Beta-Bernoulli model (placeholder)
questions.text:
Let $Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be conditionally independent given $\theta$, with $Y_i\mid\theta\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\theta)$, and let the prior be $\theta\sim\text{Beta}(a,b)$ with $a,b>0$, so that
$$\pi(\theta)=\frac{\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}}{B(a,b)},\qquad 0<\theta<1.$$
Write $s=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i$ for the observed number of successes.

parts.text: Derive the posterior distribution of $\theta$ given $y_1,\dots,y_n$, and state its parameters.

markingScheme.step: Writes the prior kernel $\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}$ and drops constants not involving $\theta$
Recognises the kernel of a Beta distribution and states $\text{Beta}(a+s,\,b+n-s)$

parts.modelAnswer:
By Bayes' theorem the posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior. The likelihood is
$$p(y\mid\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n\theta^{y_i}(1-\theta)^{1-y_i}=\theta^{s}(1-\theta)^{n-s}.$$
Hence, dropping every factor that does not depend on $\theta$,
\begin{align}
\pi(\theta\mid y)&\propto \theta^{s}(1-\theta)^{n-s}\cdot\theta^{a-1}(1-\theta)^{b-1}\\
&=\theta^{a+s-1}(1-\theta)^{b+n-s-1},\qquad 0<\theta<1.
\end{align}
This is the kernel of a Beta density, so $\theta\mid y\sim\text{Beta}(a+s,\;b+n-s)$.

parts.text: Show that the posterior mean is a weighted average of the prior mean $a/(a+b)$ and the sample mean $\bar y=s/n$, and give the weight on the prior mean.

markingScheme.step: States the posterior mean $\E[\theta\mid y]=\dfrac{a+s}{a+b+n}$ (uses the mean of a Beta distribution)
Splits the numerator and rewrites $a=(a+b)\cdot\frac{a}{a+b}$ and $s=n\bar y$
Identifies the weight $w=\dfrac{a+b}{a+b+n}$ on the prior mean and $1-w$ on $\bar y$

parts.modelAnswer:
The mean of $\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ is $\alpha/(\alpha+\beta)$, so
$$\E[\theta\mid y]=\frac{a+s}{a+b+n}.$$
Write $a=(a+b)\frac{a}{a+b}$ and $s=n\bar y$. Then
\begin{align}
\E[\theta\mid y]&=\frac{(a+b)}{a+b+n}\cdot\frac{a}{a+b}+\frac{n}{a+b+n}\cdot\bar y\\
&=w\,\frac{a}{a+b}+(1-w)\,\bar y,\qquad w=\frac{a+b}{a+b+n}\in(0,1).
\end{align}
So the posterior mean is a convex combination of the prior mean and the sample mean; the weight on the prior mean is $w=(a+b)/(a+b+n)$, which tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$. $\blacksquare$

parts.text: Prove that under squared error loss $L(\theta,d)=(\theta-d)^2$ the Bayes estimator (the minimiser of the posterior expected loss) is the posterior mean.

markingScheme.step: Writes the posterior expected loss $\E[(\theta-d)^2\mid y]$ as the function to minimise over $d$
Adds and subtracts $m=\E[\theta\mid y]$ and expands the square
Shows the cross term has zero expectation, giving $\Var(\theta\mid y)+(m-d)^2$
Concludes the minimum is at $d=m$ because $(m-d)^2\ge 0$ with equality only at $d=m$

parts.modelAnswer:
Let $m=\E[\theta\mid y]$. For any fixed $d$,
\begin{align}
\E[(\theta-d)^2\mid y]&=\E[((\theta-m)+(m-d))^2\mid y]\\
&=\E[(\theta-m)^2\mid y]+2(m-d)\,\E[\theta-m\mid y]+(m-d)^2\\
&=\Var(\theta\mid y)+(m-d)^2,
\end{align}
because $\E[\theta-m\mid y]=0$. The first term does not depend on $d$ and the second is non-negative and zero only for $d=m$. Hence the posterior expected loss is minimised uniquely at $d=m$, the posterior mean. $\blacksquare$

parts.text: Take $a=b=2$, $n=10$ and $s=7$. Give the posterior distribution, the Bayes estimate under squared error loss and the posterior variance.
parts.modelAnswer:
From part (a) the posterior is $\text{Beta}(a+s,\,b+n-s)=\text{Beta}(2+7,\,2+3)=\text{Beta}(9,5)$.

The Bayes estimate under squared error loss is the posterior mean, $9/(9+5)=9/14\approx 0.643$.

For $\text{Beta}(\alpha,\beta)$ the variance is $\alpha\beta/\big((\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)\big)$, so
$$\Var(\theta\mid y)=\frac{9\cdot 5}{14^2\cdot 15}=\frac{45}{2940}=\frac{3}{196}\approx 0.0153.$$
